title: Mori Motonari and the Three Arrows
text:
Mori Motonari was a minor lord in Aki province, in western Japan, who rose during the age of civil wars to rule most of the Chugoku region. He had three adult sons by his principal wife. The eldest, Takamoto, was his heir. The two younger ones he placed as heirs of other powerful families, the Kikkawa and the Kobayakawa, binding those clans to the Mori.

In 1557 Motonari wrote his three sons a long letter of fourteen articles, which survives. In it he urged them again and again to stay united for the sake of the Mori house, to support one another and never let any quarrel come between them, since their fortunes depended on each other.

Later tradition turned this letter into a famous scene. Motonari, it is said, gave each of his sons a single arrow and asked them to break it, which they did easily. Then he handed them three arrows bound together, which none could break. As long as the three stood together, he told them, no one could destroy them. The story resembles Aesop's fable of the bundle of sticks, and it is almost certainly a legend: Takamoto died years before his father.

The three brothers did largely stay loyal to one another, and the Mori survived the wars. Today the Hiroshima football club is called Sanfrecce, from the Japanese word for three and the Italian for arrows.
lesson: Siblings who stand together are far harder to break than any one alone. Unity has to be asked for, explained and renewed, not assumed.
people: Mori Motonari, Mori Takamoto, Kikkawa Motoharu, Kobayakawa Takakage
source: Mori Motonari, Letter of Admonition to Three Sons (Sanshi Kyokunjo, 1557); later tradition
caveat: The letter is genuine, but the scene with the arrows is a later legend.
